On the unburied dead; on the terrible poisoning of the atmosphere when their ashes are scattered into the air.

The great passage in Hegel about communities—not “states”!—that rise up in hostility against the community which has violated the unconscious root of its own strength, the divine law, by leaving the corpse unburied.
The dead person whose right has been violated finds instruments of revenge that are just as real and just as powerful as the power that violated him.
Through burial, the corpse is returned to elemental individuality and thereby raised into unconscious universality.
If the body remains above the ground, dogs or birds eat it. Or its ashes scatter through the air and poison the air we breathe.
Now other communities are rising up: Chinese, Indians, non-Europeans.
The ashes will not let us be, They drift through every land!
And then there is the decayed printer’s ink of stale ideologies. That, too, drifts through every land.
Here in the Sauerland, the mountains breathe through gills. In return, the land itself is mute. And the mountains look like turtles. The soul breathes through gills.

Because during the siege, when everyone else was working hard on the defence of the city, he busily rolled his empty barrel backwards and forwards so that he would not be idle while everyone else was working.

Magnificent dialectic: A dualism is possible only because the two partners who make up the pair are, at bottom, in agreement about something. For that very reason, the dualism ought to end in unity—if there were really nothing else on earth except this spiritual unity which, in order to sustain the opposition, requires the Iron Curtain. But the underlying unity does not exhaust the unity of the world.

It would be terrible. It would be a disaster, a horror. It would mean the simultaneous end of spirit, life, and soul if the underlying unity shared by these two parties actually resulted in a real unity.
They are two opposing sides facing each other within the same ideological world.
The common idea they share is the secret behind their division into two.
The moment this common element is recognized, the duality falls apart.
The opposition between their economic systems is only an antithetical development—two opposing applications—of the same underlying idea: a philosophy of history.
It follows that neither of these two sides in the present division of the world will be the one that creates world unity.

I do not answer questions like that without safe conduct and guarantees.
You would do better to ask:
Why have all concepts become so poisoned today—peace, humanity?
How are words supposed to preserve the identity of their meaning when the people who use them—the people in whose mouths these words live—cannot preserve their own identity?
How are these words supposed to retain the same meaning when people are forced, through horrifying mass procedures, to strip themselves of their identity?
Then perhaps you will come closer to the answer:
Because the entire atmosphere has been poisoned.
